Fit a Survival Support Vector Machine

Source: R/fit_survsvm.R
fit_survsvm.Rd

Fits a kernel survival support vector regression on the log-time scale and returns an mlsurv_model. The engine is implemented natively in survalis.

Usage

fit_survsvm(
  formula,
  data,
  type = "regression",
  gamma.mu = 0.1,
  opt.meth = NULL,
  kernel = c("add_kernel", "lin_kernel", "rbf_kernel", "poly_kernel"),
  diff.meth = NULL,
  kernel.pars = NULL,
  resid.folds = 5
)

Arguments

formula

A survival formula of the form Surv(time, status) ~ predictors.

data

A data.frame containing all variables referenced in formula.

type

Only "regression" is supported: the ranking types of survivalsvm give a risk score, not a survival time, and therefore no survival curve.

gamma.mu

Error weight \(\gamma > 0\); larger values follow the data more closely. Default 0.1.

opt.meth, diff.meth

Ignored. Kept so that older calls keep working; the native solver needs no optimizer choice.

kernel

Kernel: "add_kernel" (default), "lin_kernel", "rbf_kernel" or "poly_kernel".

kernel.pars

Optional kernel parameters, see the Kernels section.

resid.folds

Number of folds for the cross-fitted residuals (default 5); 1 uses in-sample residuals. Folds interleave the ordered survival times, so fitting does not touch the random number generator.

Value

An object of class mlsurv_model, a named list with elements model (the fitted engine), learner ("survsvm"), formula, data, time and status; the engine name "survalis" is stored in attr(, "engine").

Method

The model is an accelerated failure time model \(\log T = f(x) + \varepsilon\) with \(f(x) = \sum_i \beta_i k(x, x_i) + b\) in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of the kernel \(k\). With \(y_i = \log T_i\), \(f\) minimizes $$\frac12 \|f\|_k^2 + \frac{\gamma}{2} \sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 1} (y_i - f(x_i))^2 + \frac{\gamma}{2} \sum_{i:\,\delta_i = 0} \max(0,\, y_i - f(x_i))^2 ,$$ the survival support vector regression of Shivaswamy et al. (2007) and Van Belle et al. (2011) with squared losses: an event time is fitted from both sides, a censored time is only penalized when the prediction falls below it. The problem is strictly convex and piecewise quadratic, and is solved exactly by an active-set Newton method (Chapelle, 2007). Given the active set \(A\) (events, and censored points predicted too early), the optimum solves the least-squares SVM system $$\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1^\top \\ 1 & K_{AA} + I/\gamma \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} b \\ \beta_A \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ y_A \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \beta_{A^c} = 0,$$ by one Cholesky factorization; \(A\) is updated, with a line search, until it no longer changes. No quadratic programming solver is involved. Censored points outside \(A\) have \(\beta_i = 0\) and are not stored.

Survival curves follow from the AFT form: \(S(t \mid x) = S_\varepsilon(\log t - f(x))\), where \(S_\varepsilon\) is the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the cross-fitted residuals \(y_i - f_{-k(i)}(x_i)\): each residual comes from a model fitted without the observation's fold, so the curves are not made overconfident by the in-sample fit. See predict_survsvm for alternatives.

Kernels

"add_kernel"

Clinical (additive) kernel of Daemen et al. (2012): the average over predictors of \(\max(0, 1 - |x_j - z_j| / r_j)\) for numeric and ordered predictors (\(r_j\) the training range) and \(1\{x_j = z_j\}\) for unordered factors. Scale free, positive semi-definite, and a factor counts as one predictor. Constant predictors add a constant.

"lin_kernel"

\(x^\top z / p\) on standardized columns (factors in treatment coding).

"rbf_kernel"

\(\exp(-\|x - z\|^2 / (2 \sigma^2))\) on standardized columns; kernel.pars is \(\sigma^2\), default the number of columns \(p\).

"poly_kernel"

\((x^\top z / p + c)^d\) on standardized columns; kernel.pars is \((c, d)\), default \((1, 2)\).

References

Shivaswamy PK, Chu W, Jansche M (2007). A support vector approach to censored targets. Seventh IEEE International Conference on Data Mining, 655-660. doi:10.1109/ICDM.2007.93

Van Belle V, Pelckmans K, Van Huffel S, Suykens JAK (2011). Support vector methods for survival analysis: a comparison between ranking and regression approaches. Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, 53(2), 107-118. doi:10.1016/j.artmed.2011.06.006

Daemen A, Timmerman D, Van den Bosch T, et al. (2012). Improved modeling of clinical data with kernel methods. Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, 54(2), 103-114. doi:10.1016/j.artmed.2011.11.001

Chapelle O (2007). Training a support vector machine in the primal. Neural Computation, 19(5), 1155-1178. doi:10.1162/neco.2007.19.5.1155

See also

predict_survsvm(), tune_survsvm()

Examples

mod_svm <- fit_survsvm(Surv(time, status) ~ age + celltype + karno,
                       data = veteran, kernel = "add_kernel")
predict_survsvm(mod_svm, newdata = veteran[1:5, ], times = c(100, 300, 500))
#>       t=100      t=300      t=500
#> 1 0.4911426 0.11209330 0.04670554
#> 2 0.5367487 0.14887392 0.06538776
#> 3 0.4450980 0.09341109 0.04670554
#> 4 0.4988167 0.11209330 0.04670554
#> 5 0.5367487 0.14887392 0.06538776
